title: Trump Revives 'Public Charge' Rule That Could Deny Green Cards to Immigrants Who Use Medicaid or Food Stamps
excerpt: The policy, set to take effect September 18, broadens the definition of who counts as a 'public charge' and could affect hundreds of thousands of green card applicants — including many in the decade-long Indian employment-based backlog.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump's revived 'public charge' rule could deny green cards to benefit users.
  • Effective September 18, 2026, the rule broadens public charge definitions.
  • Hundreds of thousands of green card applicants, especially Indians, may be affected.
  • The rule excludes refugees and certain humanitarian applicants from its scope.
  • Critics argue the policy may deter eligible families from accessing benefits.
Impact of the Public Charge Rule
›Effective Date: September 18, 2026
›Affects: Hundreds of thousands of green card applicants
›Key Programs: Medicaid, SNAP, housing vouchers
›Exemptions: Refugees, asylees, and humanitarian applicants
The Trump administration is reviving the "public charge" rule, a sweeping immigration policy that could deny green cards to applicants who have used government benefits such as Medicaid, food stamps, or housing vouchers. The Department of Homeland Security announced the policy on Thursday. It appeared in the Federal Register and will be formally published on July 20, with an effective date of September 18, 2026. ## What the Rule Does Under the revived policy, immigration officers will weigh an applicant's use of public benefits when deciding whether to grant permanent residency. The programs that can count against an applicant include Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP, commonly known as food stamps), Medicaid, and housing assistance vouchers, [according to the Associated Press](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-revive-rule-that-could-deny-green-cards-immigrants-using-public-benefits-2026-07-16/). Federal law has long required green card seekers to demonstrate they will not become a "public charge" — someone primarily dependent on government support. But the Trump administration's version pulls a far wider range of aid into that calculation than the Biden-era standard, which primarily considered only cash welfare payments and long-term institutional care. The original rule, first adopted in 2019 during Trump's first term, defined a public charge as anyone who received government benefits for more than 12 months in any three-year period. That broad approach was abandoned in 2022 under the Biden administration. ## Who Is Exempt The rule does not apply universally. Congress has shielded refugees, asylees, and humanitarian applicants — including trafficking victims and those petitioning under the Violence Against Women Act, [CBS News reported](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/policy/immigration/3442938/dhs-consider-welfare-use-immigrants-green-cards/). Benefits received by an applicant's family members will not be treated as the applicant's own, though officers may still factor them in when assessing whether a household can support itself. ## What It Means for the Indian Diaspora The rule is expected to affect hundreds of thousands of applicants seeking permanent residency in the United States. For the Indian diaspora, which represents one of the largest groups in the green card backlog, the policy adds another layer of complexity to an already lengthy process.
Public Charge Definition Changes
Trump Administration (2019)
Broad definition including various benefits
Biden Administration (2022)
Narrow definition focusing on cash welfare
Current Rule (2026)
Includes food stamps, Medicaid, housing assistance
Indian immigrants on employment-based green card tracks — many of whom wait a decade or more due to per-country caps — may face heightened scrutiny if they or their dependents have accessed any form of public assistance during their wait. Immigration advocates have criticised the policy, arguing it unfairly targets lower-income immigrants and could discourage eligible families from accessing benefits they are legally entitled to, a phenomenon known as the "chilling effect." "The Trump administration is upholding the rule of law and protecting American taxpayers from subsidizing aliens who may become dependent on public benefits," USCIS spokesman Zach Kahler [told the Washington Examiner](https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/policy/immigration/3442938/dhs-consider-welfare-use-immigrants-green-cards/). U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X that the revived rule underlines the intent "that aliens in the United States be self-reliant and not dependent on taxpayer-funded government benefits." The policy takes effect on September 18, giving the agency 60 days to update paperwork and prepare for the change.
